extracted.intended_audience: patent searchers, law students, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A compiled glossary of patent-searching, drafting, prosecution, and validity terms and standards intended to explain legal and practical criteria used in evaluating patentability, prosecution practice, and searching. Includes statutory requirements, evidentiary concepts, claim-drafting conventions, and searching terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must not have been sold or disclosed anywhere in the world before a valid patent can be granted; creates an absolute bar to patentability in such countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a requirement of some patent offices, but not the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Absolute Novelty creates an absolute bar to patentability in such countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (Novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art negates novelty. Anticipation exists when the prior art indicates that a patent application lacks novelty by fully describing something within a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP references (e.g., MPEP 2131 series). Under Section 102 a claim must be identically disclosed in a single prior art reference to be rejected as anticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Bar / Critical Date
rubrics_metrics.description: A bar to patentability established by law, e.g., publication, public use, or sale before the first application; Critical Date refers to the date of initial placing on sale, publication, or public use that can start the statutory bar period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S. there is generally a one-year grace period after public disclosure; after that a U.S. patent application cannot be filed. See MPEP 2133.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness / Unobvious (Inventive Step)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of a claimed invention's not being apparent to a person having ordinary skill in the art (i.e., non-obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Section 103, one may combine two or more references to render a claim obvious if such a combination would be apparent to one skilled in the art. See also Teaching Toward and Teaching Away and MPEP references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence from the marketplace relevant to deciding whether an invention is non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories include commercial success, long-felt need, unexpected results, failure of others, and copying by others. These can support non-obviousness in view of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / Useful
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must have a constructive or functional purpose and must operate or perform as specified in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is one of the statutory requirements of an invention; see MPEP 2107 series. Utility is tied to novelty and obviousness considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) as defined by statute (35 U.S.C. §101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines what categories of inventions are eligible for patent protection. See MPEP 2105.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure / Enabling Disclosure (Enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure must be sufficient for one skilled in the art to (1) understand what is being claimed (description requirement) and (2) to enable the person to make and use the invention (enablement requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, in the U.S., the best mode of the invention must be disclosed in the application. See MPEP 608, 2161-2164.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue Experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreasonable amount of experimentation required to practice the invention from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is assessed in part by whether the disclosure requires undue experimentation. See MPEP 2164.01 and MPEP 818.03(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure in a patent application must clearly convey what the inventor(s) considered the embodiment of their invention to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description is separate from enablement and is used to show possession of the invention; see MPEP 2163.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., a patent application is required to disclose the best means known to the applicant (at the time of filing) of practicing the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 608.01(h), MPEP 2165 series; failure to disclose best mode can be a basis to challenge a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness (Claim Clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic of a patent claim in which claim language makes the scope of the claim clear to a person skilled in the art to which the invention pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be definite to satisfy 35 U.S.C. §112 requirements; see MPEP 2173 series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Define the Monopoly (Claim Drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are what the inventor states to be unique about the invention and become the actual monopoly granted; claims define the scope of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should support the claims; careful claim drafting (independent and dependent claims) controls protection. See MPEP 608.01(i),(k),(m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Phrases: 'Comprising' vs 'Consisting of'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' is inclusive and open-ended (does not exclude additional unrecited elements); 'Consisting of' is exclusive and excludes elements not specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose transitional language deliberately to control claim scope. 'Consisting essentially of' is a middle ground allowing inconsequential additional elements. See MPEP 2111.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Types and Forms (e.g., Apparatus/Process/Product, Jepson, Markush)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various statutory and stylistic claim forms exist (process/machine/article of manufacture/composition of matter); specialized forms include Jepson claims or Markush groups for claiming alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate claim form for subject matter; Markush requires members to share a defining property (MPEP 803.02). Jepson claims recite known art then the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining Prior Art (Anticipation v. Obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §102 a claim is anticipated only if a single reference fully discloses it; under §103 one may combine multiple references to show a claim is obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may reject claims for anticipation (single reference) or obviousness (combination). See MPEP 2131 and MPEP 2140+.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching Away / Teaching Toward (Evidence for Obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Teaching Away' describes prior art that suggests a claimed invention is not possible (supports non-obviousness); 'Teaching Toward' describes prior art that points in the direction of the invention (supports obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concepts are used when evaluating whether a combination of references would have been obvious to one skilled in the art. See MPEP 2145.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception and Reduction to Practice (Completion of Invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the formation of a definite and permanent idea in the inventor's mind; reduction to practice may be actual (making and testing) or constructive (filing an enabling application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completion of invention (conception + reduction to practice) and related diligence are critical in priority disputes (especially under first-to-invent regimes). See MPEP 2138 series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (for Priority/Swearing Back)
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity required of an inventor and attorney to show continuous efforts from just before an intervening reference date until reduction to practice or filing; typically includes ordering parts, prototyping, testing, preparing disclosures, hiring counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence must be proven and corroborated (e.g., by non-inventor witnesses) in interference proceedings. See MPEP 2138.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit / Swearing Back (37 CFR 1.131 / 1.132)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written, sworn statement used to remove a reference from the prior art by showing conception or reduction to practice prior to the reference (swear back) or to traverse a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits can be used to 'swear back'; declarations under 1.132 dispute a rejection. See MPEP 715-716 and MPEP 706.02 references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole Contents Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that the whole contents (not just the claims) of an unpublished application may destroy the novelty of a later application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpublished applications can be prior art against later applications under some circumstances; practitioners should be aware of how unpublished content can affect novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence Rules (biological sequence disclosure requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules promulgated by a patent office that concern the form of disclosures of inventions that contain nucleotide sequence data and/or amino acid sequence data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow sequence submission rules (e.g., MPEP 2420 series) for proper disclosure and patentability of biological sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double Patenting and Double Patenting Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper attempt to obtain more than one patent on the same invention or an obvious variant; can result in a double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections can sometimes be overcome by terminal disclaimers; see MPEP 804 series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal Disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A document filing that disclaims a terminal portion of the normal term of a patent (or otherwise surrenders term) typically required to overcome certain double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are commonly used to resolve non-statutory double patenting rejections; see MPEP 1490.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Cancellation / Amendment (Prosecution practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal or amendment of claims from a patent application is a normal prosecution activity to overcome rejections, objections, or requirements issued by the patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments should respond to examiner reasons; claims may be canceled or amended consistent with 35 U.S.C. §112/§251 rules. See MPEP 714.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal / Appeal Brief Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal is a request that a higher authority review an adverse patentability decision; an Appeal Brief must set forth arguments and cite authorities (statutes and case law) in support of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S. appeals go to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (now PTAB); briefs must comply with formal requirements (see MPEP 1205-1206).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practices for Patent Search (Search Operators / Boolean Logic / Adjacency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search techniques include use of Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT), adjacency operators (ADJ, NEAR, PARAGRAPH), wildcards, and careful class/subclass searching to assemble relevant prior art answer sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate operators and database features (e.g., wildcard, adjacency, classification, citation searching) to build comprehensive search results. Terms: AND/ANDNOT/XOR, wildcard '*' or '?', adjacency operators, classification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search Report / Opinion on Patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A search report is a list of published prior art and other references presenting an opinion as to the patentability of a particular application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search reports should include both patent and non-patent literature and be used to assess novelty, obviousness, and scope. See MPEP 707.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement (standard and consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct constituting illegal use of another's patented invention where the infringer has no reasonable basis for believing their actions are legal (i.e., knew of the patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness can justify increasing damages up to treble and/or awarding attorneys' fees; good-faith reliance on advice of counsel can be relevant to willfulness determinations.
